abstract: This study investigated muscle texture and amino acid changes in Chinese mitten crab ( Eriocheir sinensis ) during waterless preservation and further explored their relationship with physiological and metabolic profiles. During 6-days waterless preservation, significant reductions in muscle integrity, hardness, chewiness, and gumminess were revealed along with gradually decreased vitality. Essential amino acids such as methionine (Met), threonine (Thr) and valine (Val) were selectively preserved despite ongoing protein degradation, suggesting their role in maintaining basal metabolism and flavor attributes. Tissue-specific antioxidant responses were reflected by transient SOD/CAT overactivation and collapse in hepatopancreas, while sustained SOD activity in leg meat mitigated oxidative damage, delaying the deterioration of muscle texture. Day 3 has been suggested as the critical transition point from compensatory energy metabolism to irreversible decompensation, driven by lactate accumulation and antioxidant failure. Collectively, this study provides a scientific basis for quality control in the live crustacean supply chain.

Materials and methods
2.1
Experiment design
Male
E. sinensis
(150–160 g, all with intact claws) were obtained from a commercial farm in Xinghua City, Jiangsu Province. The crabs were cultured in ring-ditch ponds under standard aquaculture conditions, with a feed-to-stock ratio of 1:1500. The animal study was approved by the Institutional Animals Care and Use Committee of Zhejiang Ocean University (Approval No. 2025083) and followed the guidelines of the National Research Council for animal care. During the fattening period, the diet was shifted from formulated feed to fresh frozen fish to improve growth and flesh quality. Only sexually mature, commercially edible specimens with no visible injuries and vigorous vitality were selected. After being captured, the crabs were housed without water and had their claws and chelipeds restrained in accordance with accepted handling procedures to prevent mobility and hostility. After a 12-h period of acclimation in waterless conditions, the experimental period began with the time point known as Day 0 (0 d). Crabs were randomly placed in 6 foam boxes (each measuring 30 cm × 20 cm × 14 cm), with 8 crabs per box. The box lids contained small ventilation holes with a diameter of 1.5 cm. The boxes were loaded with an identical volume of ice cubes and the ice was replaced on a 24-h cycle. As shown in Fig. S1, the temperature (7.0–15.8 °C) and relative humidity (44.0 % ∼ 58.8 %) in the box were monitored with a temperature and humidity meter (GM1365, Shenzhen Jumaoyuan Technology Co., Ltd., China) for 24 h.
During the trial, three crabs were randomly assigned for destructive sampling and subsequent physicochemical analyses each day, which were randomly selected from three independent boxes as biological replicates. Before sampling, crabs were placed on crushed ice at 0 °C for 15 min until immobilized, and then samples were collected. Subsequently, hemolymph was collected using anticoagulant-free syringes for biochemical examination. The hepatopancreas and leg meat tissue were rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C for FAAs analysis. Sampling was performed every day. After all individuals in a group died, no further physiological or biochemical measurements were taken for that group.
2.2
Survival rate
Starting from Day 0, the survival and mortality rates of
E. sinensis
were recorded for each foam container at 24 h intervals, and the mean survival rate for each group was then calculated (
Shi et al., 2023
).
2.3
Weight measurement
Body weight was determined as described by
Wang et al. (2024)
. Three healthy
E. sinensis
were randomly selected from the foam box used in the experiment on that day, ensuring that each crab had intact appendages and no visible trauma. The crabs were carefully untied to prevent injury or stress, allowing them to be weighed in a natural state. Each crab was placed on the weighing pan of an electronic balance, and its weight was recorded using the tare method once the reading stabilized (in grams). This procedure was repeated for the remaining two crabs. The weighing procedure was performed three times for each crab, and the average weight was calculated.
2.4
Righting time measurement
The righting time was evaluated using the established method of
Maraschi et al. (2024)
, with minor modifications. Specifically, a flat, smooth experimental platform measuring approximately 60 cm × 40 cm was prepared, and the environment was kept quiet to minimize external disturbances. Each crab was placed at the center of the experimental platform, and the time taken for the crab to right itself (measured from the moment of placement) was recorded, with “righting” defined as the ventral surface fully contacting the ground. The righting experiment was repeated three times for each crab, and the time taken for each attempt was recorded. The average righting time for each crab was calculated. A video recording was also made for each trial.
2.5
Oxygen consumption rate measurement
The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of
E. sinensis
was determined based on the method described by
Bao et al. (2018)
with modifications, using a hydrostatic enclosure comprising a respiration chamber (a 2.5 L round wide-mouth bottle with a tap) and a thermostatic incubator. The respiration chamber was first filled with fully aerated tap water, after which a crab was introduced, and the chamber was immediately capped, sealed with Vaseline, and maintained at a constant temperature (25 ± 0.5 °C) for 2 h. Three replicates were established, and bottles filled only with water served as blank controls. Water samples were collected both before the start and at the end of the experiment to determine the mass concentration of dissolved oxygen using a dissolved oxygen meter. At the end of the test, the crabs were blotted dry and weighed. The calculation formula was as follows:

2.6
Texture measurement
Texture profile analysis (TPA) was conducted according to the methodology described in previous studies, with minor modifications (
Luo et al., 2021
). Briefly, crab legs of similar shape and size, specifically from the penultimate walking leg, were selected during the experimental cycle. After steaming, the crab meat was allowed to cool at room temperature for 30–40 min to eliminate the effects of high temperature, then carefully removed with a scalpel and cut into 1 cm segments. Analyses were performed using a texture analyzer equipped with a 30 kg load cell and a P25 flat-bottomed cylindrical probe (25 mm diameter) (iTexture, Zheke Instrument and Equipment Co., Ltd., China). The test settings were as follows: pre-test speed 3 mm/s, test speed 1 mm/s, and post-test speed 1 mm/s. The sample was subjected to two consecutive compression cycles at 50 % strain, with each test repeated five to eight times. Seven texture parameters were recorded at the conclusion of the tests, including hardness, springiness, cohesiveness, adhesiveness, resilience, chewiness, and gumminess.
2.7
Free amino acid analysis
The determination of FAAs in the leg meat and hepatopancreas of
E. sinensis
was performed according to the method of
Chen et al. (2024)
, with minor modifications. Each sample (2 g) was mixed with 15 mL of 15 % trichloroacetic acid, homogenized, and allowed to settle for 2 h. The samples were then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C using a refrigerated centrifuge. Five milliliters of the supernatant were collected, adjusted to pH 2.0 with 3 mol/L NaOH solution, diluted to 10 mL, thoroughly mixed, filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane, and analyzed. A high-speed amino acid analyzer (LA8080, Hitachi, Japan) was used for the measurements. The analytical conditions were as follows: a 4.6 mm I.D. × 60 mm column at 57 °C, a sodium citrate buffer solution flow rate of 0.40 mL/min, and post-column derivatization with ninhydrin reagent at a flow rate of 0.35 mL/min and a temperature of 135 °C. Detection was performed at 570 nm (440 nm for proline) with an injection volume of 20 μL. Quantification was achieved by external calibration with a standard amino acid mixture, and the results were expressed as mg per 100 g of fresh weight (mg/100 g).
2.8
Biochemical analysis
Hemolymph (1.5–2 mL/each crab) was collected from the walking legs using disposable medical syringes and transferred to a 2.5 mL anticoagulant-free syringe, refrigerated at 4 °C, and gently stirred with a syringe needle after standing for 2 h. Following centrifugation (9000 rpm for 15 min), the supernatant was collected for subsequent biochemical analysis. The resulting sample was used to determine respiration and energy metabolism-related indices, including glucose (A154–1-1), lactate (LD, A019–2-1), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH, A020–2-2).
Take an appropriately weighed amount of hepatopancreas and leg meat tissue, mix it with 1:9 (

) sterile physiological saline. The hepatopancreas and leg meat were homogenized (10 % tissue concentration) for analysis of total protein (TP, A045–2-2), malondialdehyde (MDA, A003–1-2), total superoxide dismutase (SOD, A001–3-1), catalase (CAT, A007–1-1), and total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC, A015–1-2) was determined by the colorimetric method, with results expressed in U/mgprot. All measurements were conducted using commercial kits (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, China) and read with a microplate reader as well as a spectrophotometer (
Chen et al., 2023
).
2.9
Data processing and statistical analysis
The three crabs sampled each day were considered biological replicates (
n
= 3). All experiments were conducted in triplicate. Experimental results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and analyzed using SPSS 27.0 software (IBM, Chicago, IL, USA). One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test was performed to evaluate significant differences among experimental groups. Differences were considered statistically significant at
P
< 0.05. Final data visualizations were created using Microsoft PowerPoint 16.92 (Microsoft, Redmond, WA, USA) and Origin software (OriginLab Corporation, Northampton, MA, USA), while heat maps and correlation analyses were conducted using the R software package (version 4.4.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

body:
1
Introduction
The Chinese mitten crab (
E. sinensis
), known for its unique flavor and high yield, has become one of the most popular and significant species within crustacean aquaculture industries (
Wang et al., 2025
). Consumers also highly value umami taste and high quality in aquatic products. Additionally, the
E. sinensis
exhibits notable physiological adaptations, including a remarkable capacity for survival in non-aquatic environments, which has facilitated the widespread commercial adoption of waterless transportation methods within distribution systems.
In practice, crabs are often subjected to waterless conditions during storage, retail display, or transit. To mitigate the associated stress, cooling and buffering strategies are commonly applied to reduce metabolic activity and extend survival. However, prolonged exposure to such stress can impair vitality and degrade flavor quality. This form of transport frequently results in a “live but not fresh” phenomenon that negatively impacts consumer satisfaction and damages market reputation. In recent years, changes in crustaceans quality under waterless preservation have attracted considerable attention.
Studies have found that energy metabolism in shrimp is severely disrupted under waterless conditions, leading to ATP deficiency and hepatopancreatic tissue damage (
Xu et al., 2022
). Concurrently, significant deterioration in muscle nutritional composition and fiber structure has been observed, with metabolomic and pathway analyses revealing the involvement of the neuroendocrine system (
Xu et al., 2023
). Furthermore, crayfish under waterless stress exhibited oxidative stress, impaired protein folding, and disrupted fatty acid metabolism, resulting in deteriorated muscle texture (
Shi et al., 2023
). Therefore, it is particularly important to conduct a detailed investigation into the changes in various physiological indices of
E. sinensis
under waterless preservation conditions. By studying sensitivity to stimuli, respiration rates, and body weight loss rates, integrating these with measurements of moisture content, and analyzing other observable physiological characteristics, the physiological state of crabs can be comprehensively assessed. Concurrently, changes in blood glucose levels and lactate dehydrogenase activity associated with respiratory and energy metabolism should also be measured to reflect their energy metabolism and physiological status. In waterless preservation environments, crustaceans are often exposed to environmental stresses that induce oxidative stress, subsequently affecting their meat quality and flavor (
Du et al., 2024
). Previous studies on
E. sinensis
under waterless stress have primarily focused on survival rates and basic physiological responses, such as isolated measurements of specific metabolites or enzyme activities (
Chen et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2021
). However, a systems level understanding of the correlation between antioxidant defense, metabolic dynamics, and the resultant quality deterioration remains limited. We hypothesize that waterless preservation induces coordinated changes in
E. sinensis
, encompassing physiological and morphological manifestations, muscle texture, free amino acids (FAAs) profile, and antioxidant enzyme activities. These interconnected responses are not only indicative of physiological stress but also collectively contribute to freshness deterioration through disrupted redox balance and metabolic remodeling.
This study aims to establish a scientific basis for understanding the key physiological and metabolic mechanisms underlying the decline in vitality and quality deterioration of the
E. sinensis
during waterless preservation. Unlike previous studies focusing solely on survival or single biochemical indicators, this research systematically investigates the potential “compensation–decompensation” dynamic by integrating muscle texture, amino acid metabolism, and tissue-specific antioxidant responses. It also seeks to provide theoretical support for optimising waterless transportation methods and quality control of aquatic products. The ultimate goal is to achieve non-destructive preservation and quality maintenance of crustacean products, ensuring optimal freshness, reducing losses, and supporting high quality, sustainable industry development.

3
Results and discussion
3.1
Physiological responses
3.1.1
Survival and mortality rate
The survival and mortality rates of the
E. sinensis
over the defined experimental period are shown in
Fig. 1
(a). With the extension of storage time, the mortality rate of
E. sinensis
was increasing, reaching approximately 50 % on Day 4 and 100 % on Day 6. This increasing mortality trend primarily stems from energy metabolism disruption and oxidative damage under in waterless stress (
Fig. 6
). The initial decline in hemolymph glucose indicates rapid energy depletion (
Fig. 3
a), while lactate accumulation confirms the activation of anaerobic metabolism, leading to insufficient energy supply and metabolic acidosis (
Fig. 3
b). Sustained energy expenditure coupled with oxidative stress collectively precipitate physiological collapse, ultimately resulting in death. Several studies have found that the mortality rate of
E. sinensis
increased sharply with the duration of waterless transportation, and the mortality rate of aquatic crustaceans shows a linear increase with the duration of exposure to dry conditions (
Bao, Xing, et al., 2019
;
Xu et al., 2023
). The results of this study suggest that during this period, hairy crabs experienced significant environment stress related to physiological functions, leading to metabolic imbalance and a subsequent decline in survival rate.

Changes of survival and mortality rate (a), oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (b), righting time (c), and weight loss (d) in
E. sinensis
during waterless preservation environment. Different letters within each parameter indicate significant differences at different days (
P
< 0.05).
Fig. 1
3.1.2
Oxygen consumption rate
Changes in oxygen consumption rate (OCR) may serve as a direct indicator of the physiological state of the subjects. As shown in
Fig. 1
(b), the OCR of the crabs increased after one day of waterless preservation, followed by a continuous decline from Day 1 to Day 5. A significant decrease emerged from Day 4 (
P
= 0.041) compared to the level on Day 1. OCR serves as a key physiological indicator of metabolic activities in aquatic organisms, reflecting their metabolic intensity and growth vigor. The dynamics of OCR is closely related to environmental conditions such as temperature and water content. It is worth noting that we observed that hemolymph glucose levels initially decreased and then increased (
Fig. 3
a), corresponding to the sharp rise in OCR. This suggests early energy consumption, possibly followed by neuroendocrine stress responses (e.g., CHH, biogenic amines) that mobilize glycogen, elevate glucose, and enhance heart rate and gill ventilation, thereby improving oxygen transport to sustain aerobic metabolism and homeostasis (
Simões et al., 2024
). The OCR displayed a sustained downward trend, which was likely indicative of a progressive decline in the vigor and metabolic capacity of crabs, signaling impending physiological failure. This is consistent with the phenomenon observed by
Bao, Li, et al. (2019)
.
3.1.3
Righting time
As shown in
Fig. 1
(c), the shortest righting time occurred on Day 1, with a subsequent increase from Day 2 to Day 4, indicating reduced vitality of crabs. By contrast, the longest righting time was recorded on Day 5, which further supports the hypothesis of declining physiological function. The variation in righting time was negatively correlated with the vitality of the subjects. A shorter righting time reflected better vitality, and this metric could serve as a potential indicator for assessing the health status and viability of the subjects (
Maraschi et al., 2024
). Elevated exposure to environmental stressors correlates with diminished physiological resilience in aquatic organisms, manifesting as impaired vitality and prolonged righting reflex latency, indicative of compromised adaptive capacity (
Sun et al., 2025
). The findings indicate that righting time can be used as a reliable indicator for evaluating the health status of aquatic organisms and detecting declines in their physiological performance.
3.1.4
Weight loss
The changes in body weight shown in
Fig. 1
(d) reflect the alterations in the nutritional status and metabolic activity of the crabs during the waterless preservation period. The marked reduction in body weight observed in subjects, particularly the statistically significant decline on Day 5, may be primarily attributable to accelerated water loss rather than solely reflecting daily metabolic consumption. A significant decrease in body weight was observed over time, consistent with the changes in OCR, which reflected the dynamic changes in the metabolic activities of crabs. The weight loss may not only be due to water loss, but also to a combination of metabolic disorders, energy deprivation and stress response, which may lead to a comprehensive decline in the physiological functions of the crabs, ultimately affecting their survivability and quality (
Alhoshy et al., 2022
).
3.2
Texture changes
Table 1
shows the changes in TPA of
E. sinensis
legs from Day 0 to Day 5 under a waterless preservation environment. Hardness, chewiness, gumminess, springiness, cohesiveness and resilience were determined for the cooked crab legs. The results showed that the texture properties in crab samples varied significantly at different days and the variability showed a strong regularity. The control group exhibited a higher hardness of 992.94 ± 103.09 g on Day 0, indicating a firmer texture in the fresh crab legs. Waterless preservation treatment for 2 Days had no significant effect on crab hardness. However, hardness decreased significantly from Day 3, and reduced to the lowest level on Days 4 and 5, especially on Day 5. Chewiness remained relatively stable in the early stages, declined slightly on Day 3, and then decreased significantly from Day 4. This indicates a progressive softening of the crab leg texture and a corresponding loss of chewiness. Adhesiveness remained relatively stable throughout the entire waterless preservation period, showing a slight upward trend, but the difference was not statistically significant. Gumminess decreased significantly over time. Similar to the trend of hardness change, indicating a gradual loss of adhesion and a loosening of the texture of the crab legs. Springiness and cohesiveness remained relatively stable initially. A significant decline was first observed on Days 4 and 5. In a waterless environment, crab legs gradually lose springiness and cohesiveness. Resilience was less variable initially, but it decreased significantly by Day 3. This indicated that the resilience of the crab legs gradually weakened with the prolongation of the preservation time.

The present study showed that the textural properties of
E. sinensis
leg meat significantly decreased over time in the waterless preservation environment. From Day 0 to Day 5, the hardness, chewiness, gumminess, etc. of the crab legs showed significant reductions to different degrees, reflecting the effect of the waterless preservation environment on the texture of the crab legs. On Day 0, the textural properties were better, followed by a decreasing trend in most of the indices on Day 3, and all textural properties were significantly reduced on Day 5, showing that the crab legs gradually lost the original textural properties under the waterless preservation environment. These changes can mechanistically be attributed to two primary factors. Primarily, the reduction in body weight reflects moisture loss, which compromises the structural integrity of the muscle tissue. Concurrently, protein degradation disrupts the myofibrillar network, directly leading to muscle softening. Similar patterns have also been observed in other crustacean species (
Lorenzo et al., 2021
;
Shi et al., 2023
).
3.3
Free amino acids content changes
As established by
Chen et al. (2024)
, FAAs are key contributors to the characteristic umami, sweet, and bitter flavors of aquatic products. In this study, the metabolic characteristics of FAAs in hepatopancreas and leg meat tissues of
E. sinensis
during waterless preservation were determined to reveal the molecular mechanism of the development and physiological regulation of its flavor quality. A total of 17 FAAs were identified in the hepatopancreatic (
Fig. 2
a), while 16 FAAs were detected in the leg meat (
Fig. 2
b). The umami taste was associated with glutamic acid (Glu) and aspartic acid (Asp); glycine (Gly), threonine (Thr), serine (Ser), alanine (Ala), proline (Pro), and arginine (Arg) were related to the sweet taste; whereas methionine (Met), leucine (Leu), isoleucine (Ile), histidine (His), phenylalanine (Phe), tyrosine (Tyr), lysine (Lys), and valine (Val) were responsible for the bitter taste of
E. sinensis
(
Chen et al., 2024
;
Ding et al., 2022
). Both types of tissue showed the highest concentration of sweet free amino acids (SFAAs), followed by bitter free amino acids (BFAAs) and the lowest distribution of umami free amino acids (UFAAs), while the total free amino acids (TFAAs) declined over time. Physiologically, under stress conditions, Glu in crustaceans not only contributes to flavor but is also converted into glutamine to detoxify ammonia and support nitrogen–energy metabolism, thereby lowering free Glu levels. Meanwhile, Asp can be transaminated into Glu and other amino acids via AST, and also acts as a nitrogen donor in the urea cycle, further accelerating the depletion of umami amino acids (
Meng et al., 2021
). Consequently, SFAAs tend to accumulate more abundantly than UFAAs. The results showed that the FAAs profile of both types of tissue remained intact during the initial preservation period (0–1 day), with Ala, Met, Val, Thr and Ser being consistently detected throughout the experimental cycle. It is worth noting that Met, Thr and Val were consistently detected as essential amino acids, suggesting their particular physiological importance in the stress metabolism of the organism. Concurrently, the decline in TP content in both the hepatopancreas and leg meat suggests that gluconeogenesis may have occurred, utilizing non-glucose precursors such as lactate and amino acids (e.g., Val, Ser, Thr, Met) for energy production (
Fig. 6
), as reported in crustaceans (
Liu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
). Met not only provides energy for
E. sinensis
and participates in immune modulation, but is also closely associated with antioxidant regulation (
Huang et al., 2020
;
Wang, Lei, et al., 2022
). It enhances the organism's antioxidant capacity by increasing the activity of key antioxidant enzymes such as CAT, and serves as an important precursor for glutathione synthesis. Thr and Val may also exert certain effects in immune regulation. Ser and Thr metabolism synergistically participate in the stress response of
E. sinensis
, not only contributing to energy supply but also maintaining cellular homeostasis (
Guo et al., 2022
). This process may play a pivotal role in regulating developmental responses to environmental stress. Ala participates in energy metabolism via the glucose-alanine cycle (
Fig. 6
) (
Zhu et al., 2024
). With prolonged preservation time, most amino acids exhibited a marked depletion trend. Moreover, hepatopancreatic tissues showed an abnormally high concentration of FAAs on Day 1 of storage. This is highly consistent with the metabolic mechanisms of stress in crustaceans, where
E. sinensis
meet basal metabolic demands by accelerating protein and lipid catabolism under stress (
Bao et al., 2018
). The subsequent decline in FAAs suggests their reallocation for synthesizing stress-related functional proteins or catabolism as an energy source, a phenomenon also observed in
Macrobrachium rosenbergii
during starvation (
Jiang et al., 2023
). The initial transient rise in amino acid concentration is likely due to accelerated proteolysis, as the body produces free amino acids for emergency energy. The later decline suggests some amino acids were reallocated to synthesize stress - related functional proteins. It was confirmed that the samples maintained their optimal flavor state for 0–2 days, after which the crab body maintained its vital signs but the flavor-imparting substances had fundamentally changed. This change in metabolic pattern directly led to the deterioration of the crab quality at the extended stage of preservation, as evidenced by the maintenance of optimal flavor in the samples for 0–2 days and the significant depletion of flavor compounds with prolonged preservation.

3.4
Respiration and energy metabolism
Glucose is an important source of energy for aquatic animals and is directly involved in maintaining their life activities. As shown in
Fig. 3
(a), there was a significant decrease in hemolymph glucose levels from Day 0, indicating a significant increase in energy expenditure in crabs in the waterless preservation environment, especially under oxygen deprivation and temperature fluctuations. The significant elevation in glucose observed on Days 4 and 5 following the initial decline on Day 3 indicates that the depleted glucose may have triggered glycogen mobilization, with the organism attempting to restore energy homeostasis via glycogenolysis and compensatory mechanisms. It has been documented that aquatic organisms exhibit hyperglycaemia under stressful conditions such as high temperature and hypoxia (
Xu et al., 2022
).

Fig. 3
During anaerobic metabolism, lactate is one of the major metabolites and a marker of cellular metabolism under hypoxia (
Lorenzo et al., 2021
). In
Fig. 3
(b), the initial elevation in lactate levels indicated that the crabs activated anaerobic metabolic pathways to sustain essential physiological functions under hypoxic conditions. This transition to anaerobic glucose metabolism likely contributed to lactate accumulation, a phenomenon consistent with the concurrent decline in hemolymph glucose concentrations during the early waterless preservation condition. Notably, the observed decline in lactate levels on Day 2 may be attributed to the bidirectional enzymatic activity of LDH. This finding aligns with LDH activity profiles shown in
Fig. 3
(c), where no statistically significant difference was detected in enzymatic activity throughout Days 1–3. This suggests that the enzyme system retained its normal catalytic capacity during this period, possibly alleviating metabolic stress temporarily through lactate recirculation. The observed decline in lactate levels reflects a metabolic adaptation in crabs to hypoxic stress, indicating that crabs adjust their metabolic state to cope with respiratory stress in waterless environments after prolonged exposure to such conditions (
Qiu et al., 2024
).
As the waterless preservation continued, lactate levels increased significantly from Day 3 to Day 5, indicating that the crabs may have experienced more severe hypoxia in the later stages. This could have led to sustained metabolic stress and a sharp increase in lactate concentration. The LDH activity exhibited a marked turnaround, characterized by a sharp decline to less than 50 % of initial levels on Day 4, followed by partial recovery on Day 5, but the activity remained significantly depressed relative to the initial values. The changes in LDH activity were similar to those reported by
Li et al. (2023)
and the decline in LDH, as a marker of cellular damage, is consistent with the gradual decline in viability of the crabs. The rebound in enzyme activity on Day 5 may be related to the loss of cell membrane integrity-cell disintegration during the near-death phase releases intracellular LDH into the bloodstream, leading to falsely elevated hemolymph assay values (
Ullah et al., 2021
). This provides evidence of irreversible cellular damage on Day 6 when mortality reached 100 %, despite a detected LDH activity rebound.
LDH, as a key regulatory enzyme of anaerobic metabolism, has a dynamic coupling relationship between its activity changes and lactate/glucose metabolism (
Zhang, He, et al., 2022
). At the initial stage of the waterless environment, LDH activity remained stable with no significant difference, while continuous glucose consumption and dynamic fluctuations in lactate levels indicated that the organism sustains energy homeostasis through the LDH-mediated lactate-pyruvate cycle (
Fig. 6
). By Day 4, a marked decline in LDH activity contrasted sharply with concurrent increases in glucose availability and lactate accumulation, highlighting a metabolic imbalance among these three key biomarkers. Under stress conditions, excessive accumulation of lactate leads to a decrease in muscle pH and acidification, thereby accelerating protein degradation. This subsequently causes softening of muscle tissue, adversely affecting its texture and overall quality (
Lorenzo et al., 2021
;
Shi et al., 2023
).
3.5
Antioxidant response
E. sinensis
possesses an antioxidant defense system designed to protect against oxidative damage from environmental stress, and T-AOC serves as a comprehensive parameter for assessing the antioxidant capacity of the organism (
Apak et al., 2016
). As shown in
Fig. 4
(a), T-AOC in leg meat of
E. sinensis
exhibited a dynamic pattern during waterless preservation, it remained stable during the initial phase, but showed a significant decline on Day 2, indicative of compromised antioxidant function. Although a partial recovery was observed by Day 4, the T-AOC values remained below the initial level observed at Day 0. This might reflect impaired antioxidant capacity in crabs under water deficit and stress. The T-AOC dynamics in leg meat observed in this study correspond with the typical antioxidant response of crustacean muscle tissue under prolonged stress. It is noteworthy that SOD activity in leg meat was not yet significantly elevated on Day 2. Concurrently, MDA levels in both the hepatopancreas and leg meat were significantly elevated on Day 2 compared to the control group, indicating exacerbated lipid peroxidation and substantial tissue damage caused by oxidative stress. This pattern suggests that rapid depletion of non-enzymatic antioxidants might contribute to the early T-AOC drop (
He et al., 2024
). There was then a rebound on Day 3, which was temporally synchronous with the peak of SOD activity in leg meat. This enzymatic response likely contributed to the partial recovery of T-AOC observed on Day 4, although values remained below the baseline, indicating that oxidative damage accumulated during the early phase could not be fully reversed. The accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) during this period may have caused irreversible damage to flavor precursors, thereby priming the system for subsequent quality deterioration.

This temporal regulation was complemented by T-AOC dynamics: when T-AOC decreased significantly on Day 2, SOD activity increased to maintain free radical scavenging capacity; a partial recovery of T-AOC during the decline in CAT activity on Day 4 may have compensated for the antioxidant gap via non-enzymatic pathways. This multi-system synergy resulted in a significant decrease in MDA in the leg meat on Day 4, demonstrating a greater capacity to repair oxidative damage (
Fig. 4

Compared to the hepatopancreas, leg meat relied more on SOD-dominated defense strategies, as indicated by consistently lower CAT/SOD activity ratios, which may reflect an evolutionary shift in motor tissues toward a more economical resource allocation model. The leg meat demonstrated controlled oxidative damage with significant MDA reduction on Day 4. This was achieved through sustained SOD activation, strategic CAT regulation, and dynamic T-AOC compensation. This difference may be due to the functional differentiation of the tissues, with the hepatopancreas acting as a detoxifying metabolic centre and its high frequency metabolic activity leading to a continuous accumulation of oxidative by-products (
Zhang et al., 2024
). Motor tissues, on the other hand, appear to maintain relatively stable antioxidant reserves in response to the sudden oxidative stress associated with muscle activity. In our results, SOD activity in leg meat remained at a relatively high level from Day 3 to Day 5; although no significant difference was detected among these time points, the trend indicates temporal stability of the antioxidant response. A similar muscle-specific pattern has also been reported in
Litopenaeus vannamei
(
Seta et al., 2023
).
Lipid peroxidation has been shown to be one of the mechanisms of cellular injury and the level of MDA can indirectly reflect the degree of ROS attack on tissue cells and is an important indicator of oxidative damage (
Li et al., 2017
). In
Fig. 4
(e), hepatopancreatic MDA levels increased during the early phase of waterless preservation (Days 0–3), reaching a peak on Day 3, which corresponds to the activation phase of the synergistic SOD-CAT defense system. Despite the simultaneous peak activities of hepatopancreatic SOD and CAT on Day 3 (
Fig. 4
c, d), this signalled that the antioxidant defense was approaching the oxidative stress threshold. At this juncture, the rate of ROS generation likely matched the system's maximum scavenging capacity, and this critical equilibrium state resulted in the irreversible continued accumulation of lipid peroxidation damage (MDA). On Day 4, CAT activity dropped precipitously, leading to a collapse in hydrogen peroxide scavenging capacity, but at this time MDA unexpectedly declined, possibly due to a hysteresis effect of oxidative damage or transient activation of compensatory repair. Similar findings were reported in
Procambarus clarkii
hepatopancreas (
Zhang, Xu, et al., 2022
). On Day 5, SOD activity rose abnormally while CAT only partially recovered, worsening the antioxidant enzyme imbalance. This triggered a significant increase in MDA content, indicating irreversible hepatopancreatic oxidative damage from sustained stress.
MDA in leg meat showed a progressive increase from Days 0–3 (
Fig. 4
e), which competed with the sustained increase in SOD activity and the pulsatile increase in CAT (elevated on Day 3) during the same period, suggesting that the rate of free radical generation transiently exceeded the scavenging capacity. MDA decreased significantly on Day 4, while SOD activity remained high levels and T-AOC partially recovered, suggesting that the non-enzymatic antioxidant system may mitigate the damage through complementary scavenging of free radicals. On Day 5, a further decline in CAT activity accompanied the decrease in SOD activity and T-AOC, which led to the dysfunction of the synergistic defenses and a subsequent increase in MDA. Similar patterns of oxidative stress responses have been reported in the muscle tissue of
Procambarus clarkii
under prolonged oxidative stress conditions (
Hossain et al., 2021
).
The early SOD-CAT synergistic response only slowed, but did not halt the oxidative damage process, whereas the collapse of the CAT system on Day 4 directly caused the antioxidant network to disintegrate, which finally triggered the explosive accumulation of MDA. In contrast, leg meat achieved a gradual MDA regression through sustained high SOD activity with complementary temporal regulation of CAT-T-AOC, but there was still a compensatory limit to its defense system. This difference shows that the hepatopancreas, as a core metabolic organ, is more susceptible to the “compensation-exhaustion” cycle of oxidative damage, whereas the motor tissues improve the controllability of oxidative damage through a synergistic multi-system strategy, but their reparative capacity is still limited by resource depletion under prolonged stress. Studies have reported that the muscle tissues of crustaceans exhibit greater stability and functional flexibility compared to metabolically active organs (e.g., hepatopancreas and gills) under environmental stress (
Wang et al., 2023
;
Xing et al., 2022
). The concurrent peaks in antioxidant enzyme activation, characterized by SOD and CAT peaking in the hepatopancreas alongside sustained high SOD activity in leg meat, together with peak MDA levels, indicate that the organism's oxidative defense system reached its maximum compensatory capacity. Beyond this threshold, oxidative damage began to dominate. This oxidative crisis on Day 3 was not an isolated event but the culmination of a progressing metabolic dysregulation. A shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism was initiated earlier, as clearly evidenced by a significant increase in hemolymph lactate on Day 1 (
Fig. 3
b). By Day 3, the cumulative effects of disrupted energy metabolism and sustained ROS production had ultimately overwhelmed the antioxidant defenses (
Fig. 6
).
3.6
Correlation analysis
Furthermore, the correlation analysis among different indicators related to the vitality traits and meat quality of
E. sinensis
was developed, and a separate correlation analysis was performed to specifically examine the relationship between the observed metabolic decline and behavioral or mortality data. The behavioral indicators were closely associated with metabolic alterations (Fig. S2). Correlation analysis revealed that prolonged righting time (
P
< 0.05) and increased mortality were positively correlated with glucose and lactate levels, whereas survival rate (P < 0.05) and OCR showed positive correlations with LDH activity and TP content. These results demonstrate that metabolic imbalance was closely linked to diminished vitality and reduced survival. Accordingly, as shown in
Fig. 5
, correlation analyses showed that survival rate was positively correlated with leg meat textural characteristics and was also highly correlated with leg meat and hepatopancreas UFAAs and TFAAs. In addition, the variations in FAAs were correlated with several biochemical indicators, including LDH, TP, T-AOC, and MDA. OCR showed a positive correlation with hepatopancreatic UFAAs, TFAAs, etc., but had a weak effect on leg meat amino acids. Body weight changes were highly significantly and positively correlated with leg meat gumminess and resilience, suggesting better muscle water holding capacity in individuals with better body weight maintenance. Hemolymph LDH was significantly correlated with leg meat hardness and chewiness, suggesting the effect of anaerobic metabolism on muscle texture. Hepatopancreatic TP was strongly and positively correlated with leg meat hardness and gumminess, reflecting the role of hepatopancreatic metabolism in regulating muscle structure. Overall, these findings revealed significant positive correlations between vitality traits and flavor quality in
E. sinensis
under waterless preservation environment. In particular, the strong positive correlation of survival rate, as an indicator of overall health, with leg strength and UFAAs indicated that surviving individuals were more likely to maintain meat structural integrity and flavor compounds; OCR was associated with hepatopancreatic flavor compound synthesis, whereas changes in body weight ensured meat springiness. This correlation mechanism provides a theoretical basis for optimising waterless preservation techniques, such as regulating humidity to maintain respiratory metabolism.

3.7
Potential metabolic mechanisms influencing crab muscle quality
The amino acid metabolic system of crustaceans, as demonstrated in
Fig. 6
, exhibits high evolutionary conservation with higher organisms, and its metabolic network includes the core pathways of the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA cycle), amino acid biosynthesis and catabolism, and shares the key enzymes and regulatory mechanisms with mammals. Previous studies have shown that environmental stress can significantly alter the metabolic homeostasis of crustaceans. For instance, inhibition of key enzymes of the TCA cycle after exposure to air in mud crabs triggered reprogramming of amino acid metabolism (
Cheng et al., 2020
). In this study, FAAs depletion was also observed in
E. sinensis
under waterless conditions, which was closely related to the limitation of amino acid transport and synthesis due to the down-regulation of metabolism-related gene expression. The results showed that the FAAs concentration in the hepatopancreas increased paradoxically within 0–1 day, suggesting protein hydrolases were activated at the beginning of the stress period to accelerate tissue proteolysis, thus rapidly releasing FAAs as an emergency energy reserve. This phenomenon is highly consistent with the typical stress metabolic pattern of crustaceans (
Chen et al., 2022
). With prolonged preservation, the metabolic pattern undergoes a fundamental shift, with anaerobic respiration replacing aerobic metabolism as the dominant energy source, leading to suppression of the TCA cycle and a reduction in the ability to synthesize amino acids. At this time, hepatopancreatic FAAs concentrations were systematically reduced and some amino acids were even below the detection limit, indicating that the organism had entered the “selective retention” phase. In the early preservation phase, intact FAAs profile and elevated levels of flavor-active compounds (e.g., UFAAs) corresponded to optimal flavor characteristics, whereas prolonged storage maintained vital functions but resulted in progressive depletion of key flavor determinants (e.g., glutamate), ultimately manifesting as a “live but not fresh” phenomenon. This deterioration in flavor quality is essentially due to the dual regulation of metabolic pathways - the catabolic restriction caused by the inhibition of the TCA cycle, and the direct effect of the reduced efficiency of amino acid synthesis and turnover in the anaerobic respiration mode. Further analysis of the synergistic effects of specific amino acids in energy supply, antioxidant and immune regulation will help to elucidate the intrinsic correlation between survival adaptations and flavor quality in crustaceans, and provide theoretical targets for optimising the preservation process.

During waterless preservation,
E. sinensis
may exhibit a complex metabolic adaptation that integrates energy metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and antioxidant defense systems to sustain survival under prolonged stress conditions. As shown in
Fig. 6
, initial stress triggers rapid glycolysis and partial fermentation, consuming circulating glucose and producing lactate to maintain ATP production. The gradual transition from aerobic to anaerobic respiration reduces the metabolic flux through the TCA cycle, resulting in decreased oxidative phosphorylation efficiency and suppressed de novo amino acid synthesis. To compensate for the energy deficit, proteolytic degradation of tissue proteins accelerates, releasing free amino acids such as Ala and Ser, which feed into the pyruvate metabolic pathway to support continued ATP generation. However, this strategy depletes amino acid reserves and weakens antioxidant defense capacity, as Met and Thr are simultaneously consumed for ROS scavenging and immunoregulation. The imbalance between increased ROS production and limited antioxidant enzyme capacity, reflected by fluctuations in SOD and CAT activities and the accumulation of MDA, further exacerbates oxidative damage to cellular structures, including meat proteins responsible for texture and flavor. Therefore, the combined effects of impaired energy metabolism, oxidative stress, and selective amino acid depletion gradually shift the physiological state from temporary compensation to irreversible deterioration, explaining the observed decline in both survival rate and product quality during preservation.
4
Conclusions
This study systematically investigated the physiological and quality changes in
E. sinensis
during waterless preservation, focusing on vitality parameters, muscle texture, FAAs profiles, and related metabolic pathways. Our results demonstrate a progressive decline in crab physiological status with significant texture deterioration in leg meat, particularly during Days 3–4. While TFAAs levels decreased gradually, the selective preservation of Met, Val, and Thr was evident, potentially supporting essential metabolic functions and delaying quality degradation. Day 3 emerged as the critical transition point, characterized by substantial decreases in TP content, diminished antioxidant capacity, and elevated MDA levels. Correlation analysis confirmed significant interrelationships among vitality indices, metabolic parameters, antioxidant indicators, and textural properties. These findings collectively reveal a dynamic “compensation-decompensation” mechanism where initial metabolic adaptations transition to irreversible tissue damage, primarily driven by lactate accumulation and antioxidant system failure. The maintenance of essential amino acid homeostasis appears crucial for sustaining energy metabolism and stress responses under preservation conditions. Based on the evidence, we recommend limiting the waterless preservation period for
E. sinensis
to three days to maintain optimal quality. While this study documents the physiological and biochemical changes, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. Future research integrating multi-omics analyses with sensory evaluation is essential to fully decipher the regulatory networks and conclusively validate their impact on perceived quality.
